text:
Donald Trump started a war with Iran. Now he’s ending it — and calling it a triumph.

It is not a triumph. It is not even a real deal. It is a memorandum of understanding, a ceasefire framework, a placeholder. And when you strip away the fanfare, what it actually does is reopen a strait that was open before Trump’s war started, issue waivers on Iranian oil sanctions, and hand Iran $300 billion in reconstruction funds and unfrozen assets. The 14-point framework sees Iran commit to refraining from procuring or developing nuclear weapons in exchange for sanctions relief, a $300 billion reconstruction plan, and the restarting of maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz.

That is what 13 American lives were worth to this administration.

Thirteen American service members died and approximately 373 were wounded in the weeks following the launch of U.S. and Israeli strikes on February 28. Families shattered. Careers ended. Bodies broken. And for what? To arrive at an agreement weaker than the one Trump gleefully tore up in 2018.

On the very first day of the war, a missile struck Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School for girls in Minab, Iran, during school hours. At least 165 schoolgirls and their teachers were killed — most of them between seven and twelve years old — and large parts of the school building were destroyed while classes were underway. Trump initially denied U.S. responsibility, blaming Iran for bombing its own children. The U.S. military's own initial assessment found that its forces are likely behind the attack on the school in Minab. The children are still dead. No one has been held accountable.

Here is what Trump promised: a deal better than President Obama's 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action.

Here is what he delivered: on paper, the MOU stops active military operations, lifts the U.S. naval blockade, grants immediate sanctions waivers for Iranian oil, and unlocks all frozen Iranian assets — but includes no meaningful oversight or monitoring.

Unlike the JCPOA, which enforced a strict enrichment cap, dismantled two-thirds of Iran's centrifuges, and established a snapback mechanism for sanctions, this MOU relies on vague promises and kicks the hardest issues down the road — while rewarding Iran up front.

Let’s be direct about the comparison Trump himself invited:

The JCPOA was a detailed 18-page agreement packed with technical details, the product of nearly two years of painstaking negotiation by nuclear experts and multilateral partners. Trump's MOU imposes an unrealistic 60-day deadline to finalize a definitive treaty and that 60-day clock started with Iran sitting on 440 kilograms of highly enriched uranium that the IAEA has been unable to verify, a stockpile that did not exist under the terms of the deal Trump destroyed.

Economists and energy analysts say the interim agreement appears tilted in Tehran’s favor, with Iran likely retaining significant leverage when negotiators turn to its nuclear program and ballistic missile threat in the next phase of talks.

The Iran war appears to have strengthened rather than weakened the hold of the Revolutionary Guards over Iran, even as it cost American taxpayers tens of billions of dollars, damaged our economy, drove up gas and grocery prices for working families, and sent Americans into harm's way under a president who never sought authorization from Congress.

The burden is now on the Trump administration to answer for all of it — to inform Congress and the public on the full details of this agreement, to explain its approach to sanctions relief and the $300 billion being handed to the Iranian regime, and to be honest about the true cost of a war that should never have been started.

Thirteen service members. Hundreds wounded and lives forever changed. Thousands of dead civilians. Schoolgirls buried in the rubble of their classrooms.

And what we got was a worse deal than the one Trump ripped apart.

Congress must insist on full transparency about the terms of this MOU and its implications for U.S. security. Contact your representatives and demand they hold hearings, require a full briefing, and ensure the American people know exactly what was traded away — and who paid the price.
